newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand's key finance decrees greeted cautiously.
newsitem.headline: Thailand's key finance decrees greeted cautiously.

text.p: Thailand issued four urgent decrees on Tuesday aimed at averting a crisis in its cash-strapped finance and property sectors, a move greeted cautiously by market analysts.

The much-awaited executive decrees, which the cabinet approved and become binding immediately, seek to allow greater foreign equity participation in new banks and merging finance firms as part of measures to revive the ailing finance sector.
They also dealt with the securitisation of billions of dollars in finance firm loans to the troubled property sector.
The decrees were issued as Thailand grapples with its worst economic crisis in more than a decade.

Bank of Thailand Governor Rerngchai Marakanond told a news conference that the decrees allowing a greater foreign role in the Thai finance sector would speed up consolidation of Thailand's 91 cash-strapped finance firms.

"We will be more flexible on foreign equity participation but we have not set the ceiling for this. It will be decided on a case by case basis," Rerngchai said at the joint news conference with new Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya.
Thailand currently caps foreign ownership in banks and finance firms at 25 percent.

Rerngchai said merging finance firms seeking new bank licences could seek government approval of foreign equity participation above the current limit. "Our earlier experience showed that our efforts in encouraging finance firms to merge ran into many obstacles," the governor said.
A much-touted mega merger between Thai Danu Bank Plc and Finance One Plc collapsed last month with both parties blaming tax and legal constraints for the failure.

"It appears to be a good move that the government would allow more foreign participation. It would bring in much-needed fresh inflows as foreigners reluctant to invest in the sector in the past are now given incentives to come in," said Philip Gawsawadikul, an analyst at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett.
But analysts said of the 91 finance firms in Thailand about a third were in trouble, raising the question of whether foreigners would want to invest in such firms.

"They (foreign investors) will have to be very selective and invest only in firms with good outlooks. What about small firms? If it's the Bank of Thailand's intention to see these companies collapse, it had better do something about them," Gawsawadikul said.
Finance Minister Thanong said the decrees would boost the financial sector and strengthen its long-term stability.

The decrees also detail the launch of a state-run secondary mortgage corporation to buy or refinance billions of dollars in sub-standard property loans and assets of finance firms and resell them as asset-backed securities.
Thanong said the loan securitisation measures were designed to deal with severe liquidity problems currently faced by finance companies and property developers.

"I think these moves could be quite positive in helping to restructure the industry in the longer term though in reality it is still likely to be a time consuming process," said Suraphol Thipvilai, assistant research manager at Vickers Ballas.

The decrees also smoothed out the process for merging finance companies to transfer doubtful loan accounts, waive taxes and transaction fees arising from mergers, and authorise companies to hold extra shareholders meetings to approve corporate alliances.
They bar creditors of merging finance firms from seeking court orders to stop proposed corporate alliances among these firms.

"It's positive to see they are taking these steps and getting the show on the road again, but supporting legislation would be needed to make sure they work effectively," said Sriyan Pietersz, head of research at Capital Nomura Securities.

"It's good they have allowed new banks to get above the 25 percent equity participation limit. But those who want to get involved would like to get into existing banks as a springboard to enter the market. This should be looked at," he added.
